item.title: What makes China's market so uniquely valuable?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13
What makes China's market so uniquely valuable? Tourists ride bamboo rafts to enjoy riverside scenery at the Yulong River Scenic Area in Yangshuo county, Guilin, south China's Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo/Jiang Keqing) In today's global economy, the scarcest resource is the market. Investors increasingly regard China's market as a rare asset -- even among rare assets. What sets it apart? A single word offers a useful starting point: stability. This stability is most visible in the quiet continuity of everyday life. Two comparisons help clarify why. First, the contrast with other major economies. As inflation has risen significantly in major developed economies, with prices still surging and the cost of basic necessities putting growing pressure on household budgets, Chinese consumers have continued to enjoy relatively affordable essentials. Official data supports this observation: China's consumer price index rose 0.8 percent year on year in August, a modest increase that underscores the steady rhythm of daily life for ordinary citizens. Second, the shift from past vulnerabilities to present resilience. There was a time when summer power outages and factory shutdowns were a major concern. Today, power rationing has become a rare sight. In August, China's total electricity consumption once again exceeded 1 trillion kilowatt-hours, with power demand reaching a record high. Yet cities continued to function smoothly, and homes remained brightly lit as usual. This reliability stems from a modernized, multi-layered energy infrastructure. From ultra-high-voltage transmission corridors and rural distribution networks to integrated urban microgrids, China's power system seamlessly blends conventional thermal generation with wind, hydro, and solar sources. The result is a resilient grid that keeps economic and social activities running smoothly. In a world marked by sluggish recoveries, geopolitical tensions, and volatile energy prices, such stability carries immense value. It provides a rare anchor of predictability. Notably, the International Monetary Fund recently revised its global growth forecast downward by 0.1 percentage points for the year, while raising its projection for China's growth by 0.2 percentage points. This divergence reflects growing confidence in China's economic resilience -- and helps explain why international investors are steadily increasing their capital commitments. Visitors check out exhibits at the Suzhou International Auto Show in Suzhou Industrial Park, east China's Jiangsu province, Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo/Zhang Feng) Where does this stability come from? The institutional strengths of China's system serve as its anchor. Consider the example of Dadukou district in southwest China's Chongqing municipality. Once known for its vast steel industry, the district faced a key question after the relocation of Chongqing Iron & Steel Co., Ltd.: how could it build new industries to replace the old? Drawing on its existing strengths, the district made a strategic decision to develop the motorcycle industry. The market and the government have worked in tandem. Under expedited regulatory approvals, Qianjiang Motorcycle Group moved into its new smart manufacturing facility as soon as construction was completed. Today, components supplied by Qiutian Gear are used in one out of every five motorcycles manufactured globally, while Lide Industry commands nearly half of China's domestic clutch market. Sound industrial planning, targeted policy support and continuously improving services have helped establish a well-integrated industrial ecosystem within a 15-minute radius in the city. Balancing dynamism with order is essential. With more than 350 companies competing in the same industry, how can the market remain vibrant without descending into disorder? The key lies in close coordination across the industrial chain and differentiated competition. Companies carve out specialized market niches while extending and strengthening the industrial chain, fostering closer integration between manufacturing and consumption, and between industry and tourism. From January to August this year, the industrial output of enterprises above the designated size in Dadukou district's high-end motorcycle sector grew 27 percent year on year. Motorcycle manufacturing, riding, and motorsports events have all become part of the district's identity, demonstrating how to give the market room to thrive while ensuring effective regulation. Tourists stroll through a night market in Dunhuang, northwest China's Gansu province, Sept. 26. (Photo/Zhang Xiaoliang) "Combining an efficient market with a well-functioning government" is not only a distinctive strength of China's socialist market economy, but also a key principle for economic and social development during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). By continuing to improve macroeconomic governance, upgrade traditional industries, expand emerging industries, and plan ahead for future industries, China will further strengthen the certainty and distinctive appeal of its market. The stability of China's economy is not static. It is a high-level dynamic equilibrium maintained as the economy continues to advance. Behind it lie strategic resolve and a proactive approach to shaping the country's future. "It's not venture capital, but industrial investment; not gambling, but striving," said an official in Hefei, east China's Anhui province, who remains clear-headed despite the praise the city has received for its investment success. A motorcycle made by Chinese motorcycle manufacturer ZXMOTO is exhibited at the 24th China International Motorcycle Trade Exhibition at the Chongqing International Expo Center, Sept. 20, 2026. (Photo/Sun Kaifang) High returns on industrial investment are only the visible results. The underlying strengths lie in a more fundamental approach: adapting to local conditions, making decisions based on sound analysis, and taking a long-term view. Instead of chasing every fleeting trend in a frenzy, China stays focused on innovation within chosen sectors. Instead of faltering amid headwinds, it stays anchored to the goal of fostering new quality productive forces. Instead of fixating merely on tangible, immediate gains, it devotes more to laying the groundwork for long-term returns. This poised mindset, balancing strategic steadiness with tactical agility, embodies the Communist Party of China's view on political achievements and development. It grows from a forward-evolving governance system, manifests in the tireless endeavors of hundreds of millions of market entities, and quietly shapes people's steady expectations of Chinese modernization. Such confidence in the path forms the bedrock for China's sustained and sound economic growth. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: A continuously innovating China is a land of opportunity
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13
A continuously innovating China is a land of opportunity A customer tries out a new-generation tri-fold smartphone by Chinese tech firm Huawei, the Mate XT 2, at a Huawei store in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang province, Sept. 7, 2026. (Photo/Long Wei) Chinese brands are increasingly capturing global attention in the consumer electronics sector. Early this September, they took center stage at IFA Berlin, the world's leading consumer electronics trade show. On display were Chinese humanoid robots advancing into real-world application scenarios and smart home products featuring proactive sensing and collaborative AI services. Not long ago, the smartphone industry saw a "super release week" for foldable phones. Huawei, Xiaomi, and Apple unveiled their respective flagship products within 72 hours, putting leading Chinese and international brands against each other in the same product category and sparking widespread discussion. Such moments are no longer outliers; they reflect a broader industrial shift. Decades ago, China's manufacturing base was comparatively underdeveloped. Across many sectors, the country started late, trailing global leaders in advanced technologies, standard-setting influence, and even foundational design concepts. Its early path forward relied heavily on imitation and incremental improvement. Today, that narrative has reversed. From artificial intelligence and new energy vehicles to robotics and aerospace reusability, China now competes on equal footing -- or leads -- in numerous domains. In previously uncharted territories, it has emerged as both a pioneer and a rule-maker. These breakthroughs stem from the cumulative power of scientific and technological innovation. Take the smartphone industry as an example. Ultimately, it is exclusive cutting-edge technologies that have empowered Chinese brands to march into the high-end market. Breaking free from the lower rungs of industrial and value chains represents an arduous uphill growth, as well as the continuous forging of brand competitiveness and technological "moats." None of this would have been possible without a highly coordinated innovation ecosystem. The numbers tell a clear story. The World Intellectual Property Organization recently released its report on the world's top 100 innovation clusters as part of the Global Innovation Index 2026. China, with 25 of the world's top 100 innovation clusters, maintained its position as the economy with the largest number of listed clusters for the fourth consecutive year. The Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou cluster ranked first for the second consecutive year. As a cornerstone of China's national innovation ecosystem, the vigorous development of these regional innovation clusters mirrors the steady rise of the country's sci-tech innovation strength. Progress is driven by clear strategic priorities: state support for sci-tech advancement, the cultivation of advanced, locally adapted industrial capabilities, and targeted policy incentives. A robot dances with residents in Taoyuan subdistrict, Shawan, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. (Photo/Yang Wenxiu) Equally important is the sheer scale and dynamism of the country's domestic market, which generates rich application scenarios for iterative testing and commercialization. Underpinning both is a deepening talent pool, fueled by tighter integration across education, research, and industry -- a virtuous cycle that continually upgrades the quality and distribution of skilled professionals. All these efforts to enrich the soil nurture the seeds of innovation and creativity, unleashing the momentum of high-quality development. Yet a clearer understanding of how China's innovation-driven model works also makes it harder to sustain certain misconceptions. For some time, politicians and media in some countries have been keen on hyping the so-called "China Shock 2.0", attributing China's progress in high-end manufacturing to industrial subsidies, and thereby stoking anxiety. In practice, as one international observer noted, China operates like "the world's toughest gym." Competition and innovation are embedded in its development model. Rooted in innovation, China's development brings the world not a "shock" but opportunity, not a "squeeze" but empowerment. A technician conducts tests on new materials at a research institute of storage materials in Meishan, southwest China's Sichuan province. (Photo/Pan Shuai) The evidence is mounting. Volkswagen has adjusted its R&D plans at its headquarters in Wolfsburg based on the model of its R&D center in Hefei, east China's Anhui province. Chinese AI models have ranked first for 20 consecutive weeks in terms of weekly global usage among large AI models. As a new round of scientific and technological revolution and industrial transformation converges with China's historic transition in its development model, China is pressing ahead with innovation and working to build itself into a global source of scientific and technological innovation. With such fertile ground for development, China is set to continue surprising the world with innovation. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: China leverages electric vehicles to stabilize the power grid
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13
China leverages electric vehicles to stabilize the power grid International buyers are introduced to an ultra-fast-charging battery for new energy vehicles at the 2026 Power Battery Application Ecosystem Exhibition in Yibin, southwest China's Sichuan province, Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo/Lan Feng) A global energy revolution is underway, centered on replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy and gasoline and diesel vehicles with electric vehicles (EVs). China is spearheading this shift, and developing a new power system integrating source, grid, load, and storage is an inevitable path forward. As the stock of new energy vehicles climbs toward the 100-million mark, massive numbers of EVs will transcend their traditional role as transportation tools. They are emerging as a critical component of the next-generation power infrastructure. China is expected to have 110 million to 160 million EVs on the road by 2030, with the number projected to rise to 300 million to 400 million by 2040. As ultra-fast charging networks expand, the strain of synchronized charging on local grids is becoming increasingly apparent. For instance, if 5 million EVs were to charge simultaneously overnight at 10 kW each, the resulting demand -- 50 million kW -- would far exceed the peak capacity of most municipal grids. Shifting EV charging from unmanaged, decentralized charging to coordinated, bidirectional energy flow, is therefore crucial. The key lies in enabling vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology, which allows EVs to interact dynamically with the power network. At its core, V2G transforms EVs from passive grid consumers into active, mobile energy storage units. Vehicles can draw power during off-peak hours and feed electricity back into the grid during periods of high demand. This not only alleviates grid congestion but also creates new revenue streams for owners who participate in wholesale energy markets. With an average 70-kWh battery pack, leveraging surplus cycling capacity for grid services could generate cumulative lifetime returns of 15,000 to 75,000 yuan ($2,240 to $11,198). In effect, EVs are shifting from depreciating consumer products to income-generating assets. A worker inspects charging piles for electric vehicles in a workshop of a new energy company in Luoyang, central China's Henan province. (Photo/Zhang Yixi) Battery life and safety are among the public's major concerns. Research shows that properly managed V2G operations do not accelerate battery degradation; on the contrary, they can help extend battery calendar life. Current lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries used in EVs can undergo about 3,000 full charge-discharge cycles before their capacity falls to 70 percent. Yet a typical household vehicle consumes only about 500 cycles over 10 to 15 years of use, leaving substantial capacity for additional applications. Technologies such as bidirectional pulsing can achieve more uniform lithium distribution, suppress lithium plating, and boost fast-charging and low-temperature performance. Meanwhile, V2G operation keeps batteries mostly at a partial state of charge. This prevents calendar-life degradation caused by long-term storage at full charge. When paired with intelligent risk monitoring, these systems effectively minimize safety incidents. V2G applications have already taken shape in three typical scenarios. The first is the "point" scenario in industrial parks, where vehicle batteries operate in coordination with photovoltaic generation and energy storage facilities. The second is the "line" scenario in transportation, where integrated solar-storage-charging systems and batteries used for swapping at heavy-truck stations can supply power to passenger vehicles, reducing the impact on the main power grid. The third is the "area" scenario in buildings, where integrated "home-vehicle-grid" systems enable comprehensive management of building energy use and V2G operations. Looking ahead, V2G is expected to become a major form of distributed short-duration energy storage in China. Given that high-rise buildings dominate China's urban landscape and that conditions for installing fixed energy storage systems at home are limited, using EVs parked in underground garages for energy storage is a more practical option. Electric vehicles are charged in Qingzhou, east China's Shandong province. (Photo/Wang Jilin) Under China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for the development of the new type of power system, the aggregate adjustable charging capacity enabled by V2G is expected to reach 50 million kilowatts by 2030. By 2040, as the growth of fixed energy storage slows, V2G energy storage capacity could exceed 4 billion kilowatt-hours. Conservatively estimated, the total battery capacity of 350 million EVs will reach 25 billion kilowatt-hours by 2050, enough to meet the country's electricity demand for one day in an emergency. The next five years will be a launch phase for the V2G industry. As technical standards are improved, market mechanisms are put in place and business models mature, more than 100 million EVs will effectively form a vast network of "mobile power banks" for the grid, providing strong support for energy transition. (Ouyang Minggao is an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a professor at Tsinghua University. The article was compiled by People's Daily journalist Wang Zheng.) item.title: Commentary: China's health approach advances wellbeing of humanity
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13
Commentary: China's health approach advances wellbeing of humanity BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- For a country of over 1.4 billion people, ensuring the health of its population is not merely a domestic priority, but also an important contribution to humanity. Since the 18th National Congress of the Communist Party of China (CPC) in 2012, China has further stepped up efforts in ensuring people's health, setting out the guiding principles for health work in the new era and making major decisions and arrangements for fully advancing the Healthy China Initiative. This has delivered historic achievements in the country's health sector and laid a solid health foundation for national rejuvenation. A series of facts and figures shows the profound changes in health. China has put in place the world's largest systems for medical services, traditional medicine, disease prevention and control, and healthcare security. Its health services have seen steady progress in capacity, accessibility and equity, alongside continuous improvements in people's health. China withstood the severe impact of the global COVID-19 pandemic -- a remarkable feat for a populous nation like China. The development of health services has brought concrete benefits to the Chinese people. So far, China has more than 1.1 million medical and health institutions. Over 90 percent of people in China can reach their nearest medical service facilities within 15 minutes. Its basic medical insurance covers around 95 percent of the population. In 2025, the average life expectancy in China reached 79.25 years. The infant mortality rate fell to 3.8 per 1,000 and the maternal mortality rate dropped to 13.4 per 100,000, making China one of the high-performing countries in maternal and child health recognized by the World Health Organization. China's approach to promoting people's health epitomizes the country's people-centered development philosophy. Through consistent efforts in medical and healthcare system reforms, capacity-building, legislation and health promotion, among others, China has blazed a path of inclusive and balanced health development to ensure health for all -- a solemn promise of the CPC and the Chinese government. Undoubtedly, China's all-round progress in its medical and health sector marks an important contribution to the sustainable development of humanity. As the world faces various health challenges, China has actively engaged in global health governance. China has deepened cooperation with other countries in the medical and health sector, worked together to address cross-border public health risks, solidly advanced the building of a community of health for all, contributing China's strength to the global health cause. Traditional Chinese medicine has been introduced to more than 190 countries and regions. Since late 2012, China has dispatched medical aid teams to 59 countries and regions. During the COVID-19 pandemic, China supplied a multitude of anti-epidemic products to the world. People's health is an important indicator of socialist modernization. With clear goals and intensified efforts, China will unswervingly follow the path of health development with Chinese characteristics and advance the Healthy China Initiative to secure greater progress in enhancing people's health. As a major country, China will also further participate in global health cooperation and governance to contribute more to the wellbeing of humanity. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Xi Focus: Turning China's innovation moments into lasting momentum
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13
Xi Focus: Turning China's innovation moments into lasting momentum This photo taken on Aug. 8, 2026 shows a set of home-grown brain-computer interface (BCI) products displayed at the China Sensor Valley in Bengbu, east China's Anhui Province. (Xinhua/Zhao Jinzheng) BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- In June 2024, China's Chang'e-6 probe brought back humanity's first samples ever retrieved from the far side of the moon, an achievement hailed by global media as historic. Seven months later, DeepSeek's R1 reasoning model drew worldwide attention to China's advances in artificial intelligence (AI), with a Silicon Valley venture capitalist calling it AI's "Sputnik moment." The wave of innovation milestones carried into 2026. In March, China approved the market launch of an invasive brain-computer interface medical device by a Chinese company, indicating that the device has now entered the phase of clinical application. Last week, the journal Nature published a research article reporting that Chinese scientists had developed a nuclear clock capable of stable operation, marking a breakthrough in ultra-precise time measurement with potential applications in satellite navigation and deep-space exploration. How to transform breakthroughs in individual fields into lasting gains in productivity across the economy? China has made headway in this regard, as it is pursuing "new quality productive forces," an innovation-centered major task put forward by President Xi Jinping. During an inspection tour of northeast China's Heilongjiang Province in September 2023, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, brought the concept of new quality productive forces to the public's attention, calling for better integration of sci-tech innovation resources and the development of strategic emerging and future industries. At the Central Economic Work Conference that December, Xi urged efforts to drive industrial innovation through sci-tech innovation, particularly by leveraging disruptive and cutting-edge technologies to foster new industries, new models and new growth drivers, and to develop new quality productive forces. The policy drive stepped up on Oct. 9, when the CPC Central Committee and the State Council issued guidelines setting out 19 key measures to accelerate the development of new quality productive forces. INNOVATE TO WIN THE FUTURE "Innovation drives development and innovation shapes the future," Xi has stressed. Shifting toward innovation-driven growth is imperative for China. The country has built a complete industrial system covering all industrial categories in the United Nations classification, yet it is still grappling with major pressures from demographic shifts to resource and environment constraints. The fact that some of its key technologies remain dependent on other countries, along with intensifying technological revolution and competition, adds urgency to this shift. Xi's expositions on this concept have provided guidance for the country's high-quality development as well as for Chinese modernization. At a group study session of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee in January 2024, Xi said "developing new quality productive forces is an intrinsic requirement and an important focus of promoting high-quality development." With innovation playing the leading role, new quality productive forces mean advanced productivity that is freed from traditional economic growth mode and productivity development paths, features high-tech, high efficiency and high quality, and comes in line with the new development philosophy, said Xi. From quantum technology and new energy to AI and future industries, sci-tech innovation has been a recurring focus of the Political Bureau's group study sessions in recent years. The emphasis on breaking new ground echoes a long-standing idea in Chinese philosophy. At a meeting on cultural inheritance and development in June 2023, Xi identified innovation as one of the five defining characteristics of Chinese civilization. Acutely aware of what matters for an economy with a vast industrial base, Xi has stressed that developing new quality productive forces "does not mean neglecting or abandoning traditional industries." He also stressed that developing new quality productive forces should be tailored to local conditions, warning against both a headlong rush into new industries and the neglect of traditional industrial strengths. The guidelines issued on Oct. 9 align with this approach, calling for measures tailored to local conditions and for "establishing the new before abolishing the old." An official with the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) said these principles are intended to correct problems seen in practice, including investment and planning divorced from reality, a rush into emerging and future industries, and neglect of upgrading traditional industries. FROM DISCOVERY TO PRODUCTIVITY The crucial link is turning knowledge into application. Addressing a national science and technology gathering in Beijing in July 2026, Xi summed up the relationship: sci-tech innovation should highlight an application-oriented approach, while industrial innovation should raise scientific questions. The brain-computer interface device approved in March illustrates how this works in practice. By decoding neural signals and transmitting commands to a pneumatic glove, it helps eligible patients with cervical spinal cord injuries perform grasping movements. Its market approval marks an important step toward wider clinical use. In manufacturing, the demand for better products can itself steer research. At Yangquan Valve Co., Ltd., a century-old manufacturer in north China's Shanxi Province, engineers have developed ball valves for hydrogen pipelines, opening possibilities beyond its traditional products. During a visit to the factory in July 2025, Xi emphasized responding to market demand and using technological innovation to breathe new life into traditional industries. During a November 2025 visit to south China's Guangdong Province, Xi reviewed progress in integrating sci-tech innovation with industrial innovation, and called for the building of an internationally competitive modern industrial system. He also stressed the need to accelerate indigenous innovation, vigorously support the adoption of homegrown innovative products, and foster a favorable environment for their application. China's large market, extensive supply chains and strong research capacity create opportunities to turn scientific advances into industrial applications. In Guangdong, a manufacturing powerhouse, the value added of the province's 20 major industrial clusters accounted for 31.7 percent of its GDP in 2025. In east China's Anhui Province, an expanding network of vehicle manufacturers and suppliers brings together batteries, chips, materials and vehicle assembly, making it possible to build an entire new energy vehicle without leaving the province. The broader shift is visible in national figures. In August 2026, value added by high-tech manufacturing enterprises above the designated size rose 16.7 percent year on year, compared with a 5.2 percent increase for industrial enterprises above the designated size overall. The green transition offers another marker: renewable energy accounted for 73.9 percent of all newly installed power generation capacity in the first half of 2026, according to the National Energy Administration. These changes show the scale of the transformation under way. Making the gains durable, however, requires more than successful products or fast-growing sectors. It requires an innovation system that can generate, test, finance, and spread successive rounds of advances. SUSTAINING INNOVATION, SHARING OPPORTUNITIES Xi has repeatedly focused on what happens between an invention and its wider adoption. During a November 2024 visit to the Wuhan Institute of Industrial Innovation and Development in central China's Hubei Province, he asked about development timelines, cost reductions, international competitiveness and cooperation with enterprises -- practical questions about how technology reaches the market. There is also a longer horizon. Xi has emphasized basic research, which may not yield immediate commercial returns but provides the discoveries on which future industries depend. At a symposium on basic research in Shanghai in April 2026, Xi said, "We must seize opportunities, rise to challenges, put basic research high on the agenda, advance it with sustained commitment, and strive for continuous achievements." China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) places the development of new quality productive forces and greater self-reliance and strength in science and technology among its strategic priorities. Liu Zhenzhong, a researcher at the Institute of Industrial and Technological Economics of the NDRC, noted that transformative technologies are changing how innovation is organized and how resources are allocated. Institutional reform, he said, is therefore needed to clear barriers to development. Xi has charted a practical path for empowering new quality productive forces through reform. He called for efforts to deepen reform of economic and sci-tech systems to "remove bottlenecks and blockages that constrain the development of new quality productive forces." He also urged establishing a high-standard market system and developing new ways to allocate production factors. Reform efforts include guidelines issued in April 2026 to deepen reform of the ChiNext board of the Shenzhen Stock Exchange, the country's Nasdaq-style board of growth enterprises; an initiative launched in 2024 to promote mutual recognition of data products across trading platforms; and measures aimed at improving market-access rules. Xi has also emphasized that innovation is not confined within national borders. At the second session of the 32nd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in November 2025, he stressed digital, smart and green development and called on Asia-Pacific economies to "move faster to nurture and promote new quality productive forces." He advocated deeper cooperation on open-source technologies and an open, competitive ecosystem for innovation. The core technology behind the signature substrate product of Austrian semiconductor materials company AT&S was first commercialized in southwest China's Chongqing Municipality and has since been refined there. CEO Michael Mertin said China has long made it a priority to train scientists and engineers, and the new generation of Chinese engineers "not only possesses outstanding mathematical skills but is also increasingly creative." "In today's digital age, no company, city or country can innovate in isolation," Mertin said. "High-tech progress depends on trusted global networks, cross-border collaboration, and the exchange of talent, expertise and ideas." In the latest signal of openness and cooperation, the new guidelines call for allocating advanced factors of production globally, building global networks for innovation cooperation, and establishing efficient, convenient and secure mechanisms for cross-border data flows. "The more complex the international environment, the more we should be open-minded and engage with the world. We should determine the right balance between opening up and security, and achieve greater strength and self-reliance in science and technology through international cooperation," Xi once said. item.title: World's largest ice and snow theme park to expand to record size this winter
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13
World's largest ice and snow theme park to expand to record size this winter People visit the Harbin Ice-Snow World, the world's largest ice-and-snow theme park, in Harbin, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, Jan. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Song) HARBIN, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Harbin Ice-Snow World in northeast China -- the world's largest ice-and-snow theme park -- will set a new record this winter by expanding its site to 1.25 million square meters, with a total of 400,000 cubic meters of ice and snow used. The announcement was made on Monday at the opening ceremony of the 2026-2027 ice-and-snow season promotion event, held by the Heilongjiang provincial ice-and-snow tourism development promotion association. In February this year, the globally renowned winter attraction in Harbin, Heilongjiang's provincial capital, received more than 120,000 visitors in a single day, a historic high, winning praise from domestic and international tourists. The park is expected to feature more than 1,000 ice-and-snow structures this winter, with six major sections covering ice-and-snow landscapes, amusement experiences, performances, ice-and-snow competitions, themed IP and supporting services, offering an immersive winter experience. Core landmarks such as the park gate and main tower will be upgraded. The visitor experience and performances will also be improved. "Key landscapes will be renewed, and there will be more interactive experiences," said Sun Zemin, a promoter of Harbin Ice-Snow World. In deepening the integration of sports and tourism, Harbin Ice-Snow World will work with Harbin municipal sports bureau to host a series of ice-and-snow sports events, covering curling and ice hockey among others, to promote winter sports. The theme park is now in full preparation for the 2026-2027 ice-and-snow season. China has unveiled an ambitious plan to develop its ice and snow economy as a new economic driver, targeting a total market size of 1.2 trillion yuan (about 178.3 billion U.S. dollars) by 2027 and 1.5 trillion yuan by 2030, according to a guideline released by the State Council in 2024. Leveraging the opportunity, Harbin is implementing a slew of market regulation and tourist guidance measures to continue optimizing its tourism experience, adding greater economic momentum through the use of its ice and snow resources. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Shanghai wins 1st WIPO City of Innovation award
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13
Shanghai wins 1st WIPO City of Innovation award WIPO Director General Daren Tang (L) presents an award to Chinese city Shanghai during the Inaugural Award Ceremony for the first WIPO City of Innovation award at the headquarters of the WIPO in Geneva, Switzerland, Oct. 12, 2026. Chinese city Shanghai, Britain's Liverpool and Belgium's Charleroi were announced Monday by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) as winners of the first WIPO City of Innovation award. (Xinhua/Lian Yi) GENEVA, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Chinese city Shanghai, Britain's Liverpool and Belgium's Charleroi were announced Monday by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) as winners of the first WIPO City of Innovation award. Launched for the first time in 2026, the WIPO City of Innovation award is open to cities across all 194 WIPO member states and is bestowed on visionary cities for their bold pledges to foster innovation and creativity over the coming year. The three winners were chosen from 15 finalist cities. According to WIPO, Shanghai's vision is to strengthen its position as an international hub for science, technology and intellectual property (IP), while fostering a broader culture of innovation and creativity. Its pledges include expanding IP education and services, opening innovation infrastructure and data, supporting cultural and creative industries, and strengthening connections between research, industry, entrepreneurs and investors. Zhou Yaming, Deputy Secretary-General of the Shanghai Municipal People's Government, said the award represents WIPO's strong recognition of Shanghai's innovative developments and its efforts in building a thriving IP ecosystem. "It also reflects the international community's endorsement of China's commitment to open innovation, mutual benefits and shared success," He said. Winners were selected by an independent international jury of high-profile experts in the cultural and creative sectors, urban planning, community development, and innovation-driven growth. Andrea Dempster Chung, member of the International Jury Panel and Co-Founder & Executive Director for Kingston Creative, said Shanghai's application was extremely impressive, not just because of its strong research and development base that the city already had, but for the sheer scale of its ambitions and the strength of pledges. "This would be pivotal in shifting the city's future and this is one of the reasons why Shanghai was selected," she said. item.title: China rolls out "token factories" to drive AI economy
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13
China rolls out "token factories" to drive AI economy This photo provided by iSoftStone Information Technology (Group) Co., Ltd. shows a scene inside a token factory at the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 21, 2026. (Xinhua) BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- As AI applications gain momentum, China is accelerating the rollout of "token factories" in a bid to build an economic order suited to the AI era. Every time a user prompts an AI model to generate code, images or video, tokens are consumed behind the scenes. In March, China adopted "ciyuan" as the official Chinese term for "token," giving its AI services a standard unit for measuring, settling and tracking usage -- similar to how electricity is measured in kilowatt-hours. In late September, Beijing unveiled an action plan to accelerate the development of the token economy for 2026-2028. "This is the first provincial-level policy in China specifically dedicated to the token economy," said Zhang Jinrui, an official with the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology. "With the rollout of Beijing's new policy, tokens are no longer just a technical term associated with large models. The token economy has officially entered a stage of industrial application and institutional development," said Liu Yong, president of the Beijing-based Zhongguancun Internet Finance Institute. The Beijing action plan calls for building world-class token factories and establishing tiered evaluation standards, with throughput capacity, time to first token, PUE (power usage effectiveness) and cache hit rate as core metrics, to ensure the large-scale supply of high-quality tokens. A token factory can be thought of as the AI era's equivalent of a power plant. It integrates electricity, chips, data and models to directly produce tokens. Unlike traditional data centers that only rent out computing cards, customers no longer need to deploy models or optimize inference themselves -- they simply pay for the tokens they use. In the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area, the Chinese capital's first token factory is now in operation, with a daily capacity of up to 1.4 trillion tokens in its first phase. The plan also designates token distribution platforms as part of the city's new infrastructure layout, exploring market-based pricing and circulation mechanisms for tokens, so that tokens can truly be measured and traded as an economic factor. On the application side, the new policy encourages the development of general-purpose and industry-specific AI agents, bringing token capabilities into sectors such as industry, research and government affairs. Chen Guangming, an official with the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology, said token consumption is currently growing fastest in AI-generated content and programming, and more vertical industries will become potential growth drivers for token consumption in the future. "In the internet era, competition was all about traffic and user attention. In the AI era, the logic has shifted -- what matters now is the quality and efficiency of outputting effective tokens," Liu said, adding that the shift from a traffic economy -- one built on user visits and attention -- to a token economy represents a new trend in China's economic development. Data from China's National Data Administration shows that by June, the country's average daily token calls had surpassed 500 trillion. "More than half of those calls were made in Beijing," Zhang said, noting that the city has so far registered 242 large models for public use. Beijing's early push is aimed not merely at building a series of token factories, but at exploring institutional rules suited to the token economy, making the city a testing ground for the industry's development, according to local authorities. Elsewhere, localities across China are developing token economies tailored to their own strengths, as part of efforts to implement the State Council's guidelines on the "AI Plus" initiative. The guidelines aim to build a systematic support framework for AI covering models, data, computing power, applications, open-source development, talent, policies and regulations, and security. In May, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, drawing on its green computing resources, launched a token trading platform integrating model calls, token matching and transaction settlement. Nanning, capital of south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, is exploring new models such as cross-border data compliance and remote model inference delivery, helping domestic computing power and large-model capabilities reach ASEAN markets as standardized token services. East China's Anhui Province, meanwhile, encourages banks to offer "token loans" as a financial tool for the token economy. Industry observers generally agree that the global token economy remains in its early stage but holds vast potential. A research report by CICC, a Chinese investment bank, sees "token factories" as one of the fastest-growing and most commercially promising business models for large-model developers in the near term. JPMorgan predicts that China's AI inference token consumption will grow about 370-fold between 2025 and 2030. China's three major telecom operators rolled out token packages in May for individual users as well as government and enterprise clients, bringing token commercialization further into reach for individual consumers. Li Lingran, an engineer at an internet company in Beijing, says using large AI models at work has become as essential as water. He now spends more than 200 yuan (about 30 U.S. dollars) a month on tokens, even more than his traditional mobile phone bill. "This is a shift you can't ignore," he said. item.title: Xi calls for decisive progress in Healthy China advancement
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13
Xi calls for decisive progress in Healthy China advancement Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, delivers an important speech during a national meeting on health in Beijing, capital of China. The meeting was held in Beijing on Monday and Tuesday. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi) BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for efforts to firmly follow a path with Chinese characteristics in developing the country's health programs, to secure decisive progress in the Healthy China Initiative over the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks at a national meeting on health held in Beijing on Monday and Tuesday. Xi stressed that people's health is a key benchmark of a nation's prosperity and strength. Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, the Party has made a major decision to launch the Healthy China Initiative, promoting the establishment of the world's largest systems of medical services, traditional medicine, disease prevention and control, and healthcare security, said Xi, noting that the country has achieved historic accomplishments and made all-round progress in healthcare. He said the goal is to build a Healthy China, where health services are ensured in a balanced, inclusive, high-quality and efficient manner. Xi stressed that people's health should be factored into all policies and reflected in every aspect of work. Prevention, he said, is the most cost-effective and efficient approach to protecting public health. He called for greater emphasis on foundational health work, addressing risks at their source, and encouraging the public to adopt a sound understanding of health and take an active role in managing their own well-being. He also called for a stronger disease prevention and control system to guard against large-scale outbreaks. Xi underscored the need to optimize the functions and structural layout of medical institutions so that people can access medical care close to home and receive effective treatment. He also urged efforts to improve mechanisms for the preservation and innovative development of traditional Chinese medicine, strengthen basic research and original innovation in the health sector, and enhance the patient experience. Xi stressed that coordinating the development and regulation of medical services, medical insurance, and pharmaceuticals should be a key priority in reforming China's medical and healthcare systems. He also called for efforts to train and develop a sufficient number of highly qualified medical professionals. Efforts will also be made to actively promote the building of a global community of health for all, work with other countries to address major challenges in the health sector, and continuously improve the health and well-being of people around the world, he said. The meeting was held in Beijing on Monday and Tuesday. Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang and Li Xi attended the meeting.
